source_title: The More You Buy, The More You Lose
other_side: Zitron published the same day and does not engage the open-weight argument at all — no mention of the letter, of Kimi, or of Anthropic's refusal to sign. What he does contest is the premise underneath it: that these companies are large, healthy actors whose commercial interests happen to point at a public good. He takes this edition's lead headline, NVIDIA's investment in Safe Superintelligence, and files it under manufactured demand, describing SSI as "a company with no products or plans other than to rent NVIDIA GPUs", and reads the reported $250bn backstop for a SoftBank-affiliate data centre as "the final boss of circular financing". His argument is that hyperscalers cannot stop spending without being graded on what they bought, so the coordination we are watching — investments, guarantees, joint letters — is what an industry does when genuine paying demand is thinner than the capex requires.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether coordinated corporate behaviour in AI reflects real demand or manufactured demand. Both accept the same facts — NVIDIA's $750bn of new deals, the SSI investment, and that public positions track commercial positions; NLW's own guest calls the letter eight trillion dollars of market cap acting because it is good for their business. The empirical question that will resolve is whether the backstopped capacity is built and paid for by customers rather than by guarantees, and the observable is whether SB Energy raises the debt and energises meaningful load. The residue is worldview: NLW sees self-interest converging with a public good, Zitron sees an industry that cannot find buyers. NLW is vindicated if open-weight competition and the build-out proceed on their own money; Zitron if vendor guarantees keep paying. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW's show needs the fight to matter, Zitron's subscribers need collapse to be certain — and the signal is that both, from opposite priors, treat commercial self-interest as the honest explanation of the letter. Watch whether that site breaks ground.
